B: the bracelet runs diagonally across the card, and its open center leaves less mass, but it holds the same margin (about 0.115). A: the jacket fills the card compactly at 0.84 × 0.65, with the sash running diagonally and the sleeves well clear of the edges. B: the hat is a thin horizontal strip, 0.921 wide and 0.475 tall, both outside the real range. Its brim nearly touches both sides, with empty sky above and below. This is a weak lean, because a wide brim explains part of the shape.
pairs.fix: Turn the hat three-quarters and tilt the crown toward the viewer so it stands taller and fills more of the card's height, with the brim clear of the left and right edges.

pairs.difference: A: the beach ball is one huge mass filling the card (area 0.493, just above the range), and it is named instantly, with the sand staying quiet. pairs.difference: A: the thin rope gives only 0.153 subject area, far below the real range, and the loop outline is mostly empty green. The wooden beam, cropped by the left and right edges, is the heaviest shape on the card and competes with the coil. B: the pair of sneakers sits low (box height 0.487, also short) with empty orange above, but the shoes are one solid, instantly named mass.

Little sky is left around the frontal block, so the card feels dense, and many small windows and rails compete at thumbnail size. Area (0.466 and 0.465) and margins are almost identical, and both vehicles are named instantly. They sit in the same range and use the same scene-style framing as the real plane and taxi.

A: the wheel is cropped by the right and bottom edges, with the hub at lower right. Three fields fall outside the range (area 0.477, height 0.898, margin 0), yet the crop and hub position match the real Ferris wheel card in image 1. B: the jellyfish is whole and clear of the edges, with an area of 0.245 from thin tentacles and a few small bubbles at the sides. Its bell reads first, and that framing is also real-like. Composition gives no reason to choose.

pattern: On this vector, generated cards give themselves away by less decisive framing, and the signal is weak. In the lessons, the model keeps the whole object in frame, centered and frontal, with even margins, or it adds supporting scene elements. Examples are the extra rocks and props around the lighthouse, where the real card crops the base at the bottom edge. In the test pairs, the likeliest giveaways are a second element that outweighs or competes with the hero, such as the campfire under the pot, the beam under the rope and the fence around the saddle. Others are a hero that is too sparse or too dense for the card, such as the thin rope (area 0.153) and the saloon (area 0.631). Real cards commit to one mass with quiet surroundings, even when that means cropping it. Most pairs stay close on the metrics, so composition alone leaves only low-confidence calls; several were called neither.
